concepts.def: The system composed of glands which secrete chemicals called hormones directly into the bloodstream.
A chemical secreted by a gland directly into the bloodstream; the blood carries the hormone to a target organ where it produces an effect.
Compared to the nervous system, the effects brought about by the endocrine system are slower but act for longer.

A 'master gland' in the brain which secretes several hormones into the blood in response to body conditions; these hormones in turn act on other glands to stimulate other hormones to be released to bring about effects.

On a diagram of the human body: the pituitary gland is in the brain; the thyroid is in the neck; the adrenal glands are on top of the kidneys; the pancreas lies behind the stomach; the ovaries are in the lower abdomen; the testes are below the abdomen in the scrotum.
The gland that monitors and controls blood glucose concentration by producing hormones.
The hormone produced by the pancreas if the blood glucose concentration is too high; it causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells.
The storage substance made in liver and muscle cells, where excess glucose is converted to glycogen for storage.
A disorder in which the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin, characterised by uncontrolled high blood glucose levels and normally treated with insulin injections.
A disorder in which the body cells no longer respond to insulin produced by the pancreas; a carbohydrate controlled diet and an exercise regime are common treatments, and obesity is a risk factor.
The hormone produced by the pancreas if the blood glucose concentration is too low; it causes glycogen to be converted into glucose and released into the blood.

Control in which a level that has moved away from normal brings about a response that returns it to normal; it controls blood glucose through insulin and glucagon, the water level through ADH, and thyroxine levels.
The features that develop during puberty, caused by reproductive hormones.
The main female reproductive hormone, produced in the ovary; with progesterone it is involved in maintaining the uterus lining.
The release of an egg from the ovary; from puberty eggs begin to mature and one is released approximately every 28 days.
The main male reproductive hormone, produced by the testes; it stimulates sperm production.
A hormone involved in the menstrual cycle which causes maturation of an egg in the ovary.
A hormone involved in the menstrual cycle which stimulates the release of the egg.
A hormone involved in the menstrual cycle which, with oestrogen, is involved in maintaining the uterus lining.

Methods of controlling fertility that use hormones: oral contraceptives that contain hormones to inhibit FSH production so that no eggs mature; and injection, implant or skin patch of slow release progesterone to inhibit the maturation and release of eggs for a number of months or years. Some intrauterine devices also release a hormone.

Methods of controlling fertility that do not use hormones: barrier methods such as condoms and diaphragms which prevent the sperm reaching an egg; intrauterine devices which prevent the implantation of an embryo; spermicidal agents which kill or disable sperm; abstaining from intercourse when an egg may be in the oviduct; and surgical methods of male and female sterilisation.
A drug containing FSH and LH given to a woman to treat infertility, after which she may become pregnant in the normal way.

Fertility treatment in which a mother is given FSH and LH to stimulate the maturation of several eggs; the eggs are collected from the mother and fertilised by sperm from the father in the laboratory, the fertilised eggs develop into embryos, and at the stage when they are tiny balls of cells one or two embryos are inserted into the mother's uterus. It is very emotionally and physically stressful, the success rates are not high, and it can lead to multiple births which are a risk to both the babies and the mother.

A hormone produced by the adrenal glands in times of fear or stress; it increases the heart rate and boosts the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles, preparing the body for 'flight or fight'.
A hormone from the thyroid gland which stimulates the basal metabolic rate and plays an important role in growth and development; its level is controlled by negative feedback.

mcqs.q: A gland of the endocrine system secretes a hormone. How does that hormone reach the organ where it produces an effect, and how do its effects compare with those of the nervous system?
options: carried along nerves; effects are slower but last longer
carried in the blood; effects are faster but end much sooner
carried along nerves; effects are faster but end sooner
carried in the bloodstream; effects are slower but last longer
mcqs.explain: Glands secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream and the blood carries the hormone to a target organ; compared to the nervous system the effects are slower but act for longer.

mcqs.q: A student labels endocrine glands on a diagram of the human body. Which label has been placed in the correct position?
options: the adrenal gland labelled inside the brain
the thyroid gland labelled in the neck
the pituitary gland labelled below the stomach
the pancreas labelled near the base of the brain
mcqs.explain: The thyroid is found in the neck, and students should be able to identify its position on a diagram of the human body.

mcqs.q: Why is the pituitary gland described as a 'master gland'?
options: its hormones make other glands release hormones
its hormones produce all the body effects directly
its hormones travel to the glands along nerves
its hormones act on every organ in the body
mcqs.explain: The pituitary gland secretes several hormones into the blood in response to body conditions, and these act on other glands to stimulate other hormones to be released.

mcqs.q: After a meal, the blood glucose concentration of a person who does not have diabetes rises above the normal level. What happens next?
options: insulin is released and glycogen forms in the blood
insulin is released so that glucose leaves the cells
no insulin is released, so glucose is not moved into the cells
insulin is released and glucose enters the cells
mcqs.explain: If the blood glucose concentration is too high, the pancreas produces the hormone insulin that causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells.

mcqs.q: A person's blood glucose concentration is too high. What happens to the excess glucose?
options: it is changed into glycogen in the blood
it is released from the cells into the blood
it is changed into glycogen by glucagon
it moves into cells and is stored as glycogen
mcqs.explain: Insulin causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells, and in liver and muscle cells excess glucose is converted to glycogen for storage.

options: the body cells stop responding to insulin
the pancreas releases insulin when glucose is low
the pancreas fails to produce enough insulin
the pancreas is affected by a person's diet
mcqs.explain: Type 1 diabetes is a disorder in which the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin, and it is characterised by uncontrolled high blood glucose levels.

mcqs.q: A person with Type 2 diabetes has a normal concentration of insulin in the blood but a high blood glucose concentration. Why?
options: their pancreas has completely stopped making insulin
their insulin cannot act on glucose in the blood
their body cells no longer respond to insulin
their insulin is released when blood glucose is low
mcqs.explain: In Type 2 diabetes the body cells no longer respond to insulin produced by the pancreas, so glucose is not moved from the blood into the cells even though insulin is present.

mcqs.q: A graph shows blood glucose concentration for two hours after a glucose drink. For a person without diabetes the concentration rises to a peak and then returns to its starting level. For a person with untreated Type 1 diabetes it rises higher and stays high. What does the graph show about the person with Type 1 diabetes?
options: not enough insulin is produced to lower blood glucose
their body cells have stopped responding to insulin
their insulin cannot change glucose to glycogen
their insulin is produced when glucose is low
mcqs.explain: The concentration stays high because the pancreas fails to produce sufficient insulin, so glucose is not moved from the blood into the cells and the level is not brought back down.

mcqs.q: Several hours after a meal, the blood glucose concentration of a person falls below the normal level. Which change restores it?
options: insulin is released and stored glycogen changes to glucose
glucagon is released and the glucose changes to glycogen
glucagon is released and glycogen changes to glucose
insulin is released and the glucose changes to glycogen
mcqs.explain: If the blood glucose concentration is too low, the pancreas produces glucagon, which causes glycogen to be converted into glucose and released into the blood.

mcqs.q: What is the role of follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) in the menstrual cycle?
options: it causes a mature egg to be released
it keeps the lining of the uterus in place
it causes an egg to mature in the ovary
it is made in the pituitary gland, as oestrogen is
mcqs.explain: Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) causes maturation of an egg in the ovary.

mcqs.q: Which interaction between hormones helps to control the menstrual cycle?
options: LH inhibits FSH and causes an egg to mature
FSH inhibits oestrogen and maintains the lining
progesterone stimulates FSH and LH release
oestrogen inhibits FSH and stimulates LH release
mcqs.explain: Oestrogen produced in the ovary inhibits the production of FSH and stimulates the release of LH, which then stimulates the release of the egg.

mcqs.q: A graph of hormone levels during the menstrual cycle shows the level of LH rising to a sharp peak on day 14. What is happening on day 14?
options: an egg is starting to mature in the ovary
an egg is being released from the ovary
the lining of the uterus is being maintained
the uterus lining is breaking down
mcqs.explain: Luteinising hormone (LH) stimulates the release of the egg, so a sharp peak in LH on day 14 indicates ovulation.

mcqs.q: A woman wants a method of contraception that does not use hormones. Which method and reason are correct?
options: a condom, which releases a hormone slowly
a diaphragm, which stops sperm reaching eggs
the pill, which kills sperm before they arrive
a spermicide, which prevents an embryo implanting
mcqs.explain: Barrier methods such as condoms and diaphragms prevent the sperm reaching an egg, so they control fertility without using hormones.

mcqs.q: How do oral contraceptives that contain hormones prevent pregnancy?
options: they inhibit FSH production so no eggs mature
they kill or disable sperm before fertilisation
they inhibit FSH so the uterus lining breaks down
they inhibit LH so that no eggs mature
mcqs.explain: Oral contraceptives contain hormones to inhibit FSH production so that no eggs mature.

mcqs.q: A woman does not release eggs because her level of FSH is too low. Which treatment could allow her to become pregnant in the normal way?
options: a fertility drug that contains FSH and LH
a fertility drug that contains progesterone
IVF, in which eggs are fertilised in her body
a fertility drug that contains only LH
mcqs.explain: Giving FSH and LH in a 'fertility drug' to a woman stimulates the maturation and release of eggs, and she may then become pregnant in the normal way.

mcqs.q: Which statement about IVF treatment is correct?
options: eggs are fertilised by sperm in the laboratory
eggs are fertilised by the sperm inside the mother
most IVF treatments result in a successful birth
multiple births from IVF carry very little risk
mcqs.explain: In IVF the eggs are collected from the mother and fertilised by sperm from the father in the laboratory; the embryos are inserted into the uterus as tiny balls of cells.

mcqs.q: A student is suddenly frightened by a loud noise. Which gland releases adrenaline, and what effect does it have?
options: the adrenal gland; it speeds up the heart rate
the pituitary gland; it speeds up the heart rate
the thyroid gland; it reduces the heart rate
the pituitary gland; it lowers the heart rate
mcqs.explain: Adrenaline is produced by the adrenal glands in times of fear or stress; it increases the heart rate and boosts the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles.

mcqs.q: The concentration of thyroxine in the blood of a person rises above the normal level. What happens next?
options: more thyroxine is released and the level rises
the metabolic rate falls and the level stays high
the metabolic rate falls and thyroxine forms
thyroxine release is inhibited and the level falls
mcqs.explain: Thyroxine levels are controlled by negative feedback, so a level above normal inhibits the release of thyroxine until the level returns to normal.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the main reproductive hormones is correct?
options: oestrogen is produced by the pituitary gland
testosterone is produced by the testes
oestrogen is produced by the thyroid gland
testosterone is produced by the pituitary
mcqs.explain: Testosterone is the main male reproductive hormone produced by the testes, and it stimulates sperm production.
